There is also evidence that commercial zone and terminal area expansion will reduce the need of shippers to turn to private carriage to the benefit of for-hire motor carriers. Evidence presented relating to the comparative incidence of private carriage at industrial parks inside and outside the Philadelphia commercial zone supports this thesis. Similar information resulted from the DOT study of the effects of the expansion of the Baltimore commercial zone. Many suburban shippers stated that if zone limits were expanded, they would not be compelled to enter into private carriage. Since small shippers do not ordinarily have the financial ability to exercise the private carriage option, the reduction of private carriage through zone expansion should aid in evening out the respective positions of large and small shippers from a transportation standpoint.

The January 12, 1976, issue of <u>Traffic World</u>, contained an article dealing with the trend toward satellite suburban terminals in the Chicago area (see p. 17). The primary reasons cited for this trend were the high operating costs and traffic congestion in the city and the movement of industry to the suburbs. The dispersion of industry has increased pickup and delivery travel time, often without a concomitant increase in service charges. It was also indicated that shippers are becoming less tolerant of delays when freight must move into Chicago before dispatching to outlying commercial locations.
